title: Real-to-Integer Reduction for All-Pairs Shortest Paths

blocks.heading: Abstract
blocks.text: Efficient graph algorithms often use techniques that are specific to integer-valued inputs and do not work for real-valued versions of the problems. Is it a limitation of current techniques, or are the real-valued variants inherently harder? One way to study this question is through real-to-integer reductions. We give (randomized, combinatorial) subcubic real-to-integer reductions for two central graph problems in fine-grained complexity: All-Pairs Shortest Paths and Exact Triangle. That is, we show that if the integer variants of these problems can be solved in truly subcubic time, then the real variants can also be solved in truly subcubic time. Our work extends and combines techniques from three previous works: (1) our real-to-integer reduction for the 3SUM problem (Fischer, Polak, Schmidt, FOCS 2026), which itself combines the Frank--Tardos theorem from optimization with Freiman's theorem from additive combinatorics; (2) universe reduction for APSP (Fischer, STOC 2026), which we generalize to reals and use to reduce the doubling of the set of edge weights; and (3) the ``Fredman's trick meets dominance product'' technique (Chan, Vassilevska Williams, Xu, STOC 2023), which is needed to adapt the prior real-to-integer framework from equality constraints to inequalities. As a corollary, our reduction combined with Yuval's fast Integer APSP algorithm in the real RAM model with multiplication (IPL 1976) shows that the Real APSP Hypothesis is false in this model, which also follows from the very recent breakthrough by Alman and Vassilevska Williams using a very different approach.

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: When designing fast algorithms for (weighted) graph problems, we have available many techniques that work only for integer edge weights, e. g., scaling [Gabow85], bit-based priority queues [Boas75, AhujaMOT90], encoding weights as polynomial exponents [AlonGM97], or iterative methods whose convergence hinges upon integrality [Ford56]. Many graph problems seem to become substantially harder when we allow for real-valued weights. A classic example of this phenomenon is the negative-weight Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) problem: for integer edge weights, an improvement over the textbook O(nm) -time Bellman Ford algorithm was found already in the 1980s [Gabow85], and now we know a near-linear time algorithm [BernsteinNW25], whereas for real edge weights the first improvement over Bellman Ford came only in 2024 [Fineman24] and the existence of an tilde O(n+m) -time algorithm is still open. The maximum flow problem has a similar history [GoldbergR98, ChenKLPGS25], but there only polylogarithmic improvements over the O(nm) running time are known for real-valued capacities [CheriyanHM90, Orlin13]

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: The main focus of this paper is another fundamental graph problem, the All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) problem. Given a directed edge-weighted graph G=(V, E, w), with no negative cycles, the APSP problem asks to compute the length of a shortest path from u to v for every pair of vertices (u, v) in V times V. APSP is one of the central problems in fine-grained complexity [VassilevskaW18, Vassilevska18]. The textbook Floyd Warshall algorithm [Floyd62a, Warshall62, Roy59] solves it in time O(n^3), and for a long time, until the very recent O(n^(2. 9995)) -time breakthrough algorithm [AlmanV26], only a subpolynomial 2^(O( log n )) improvement was known [Williams18]. This state of affairs led people to study APSP through the lens of subcubic reductions i. e., reductions that show that a truly subcubic algorithm for one problem yields a truly subcubic algorithm for another problem and many problems are now known to be equivalent to APSP under such reductions [VassilevskaW18, TamakiT98, BackursDT16, AbboudGW23, BringmannGMW18, NoglerPSVWXY25]

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: For APSP, the difference between integer- and real-valued inputs is less immediately visible, because the best known algorithms (both currently and historically) have the same running times. However, the techniques differ substantially. For instance, the paper of Williams [Williams18] begins with "a succinct exposition of a good algorithm for APSP, at least in the case of reasonable-sized [integer] weights", which is followed by a much longer description of the full algorithm for real-valued inputs. Also, the recent breakthrough truly subcubic algorithm for integer inputs is deterministic while for reals it is randomized [AlmanV26]

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: This phenomenon, for APSP and other problems, begs to ask a question: start-of-center: Are integer-only tricks a necessity or just a convenience? end-of-center

blocks.heading: Introduction
blocks.text: We remark that this distinction is related, but not equivalent, to the distinction between algorithms whose running time is weakly-polynomial (i. e., it depends polynomially on the bit-length of input numbers) and strongly-polynomial (i. e., it does not depend on the size of input numbers). Often, a strongly-polynomial time algorithm for integers would also work for reals, but this is not always the case (e. g., [BaranDP08] )

blocks.heading: Our Results
blocks.text: We address the above question in the case of APSP by providing a real-to-integer subcubic reduction

blocks.heading: Our Results
blocks.text: start-of-theorem: [Real-to-Integer Reduction for APSP] If Integer APSP, with edge weights from (-u, dots, u), can be solved in time O(n^(3-epsilon)(log u)^(O(1))) for some constant epsilon > 0, then Real APSP can be solved in time O(n^(3-Omega(epsilon^3))), by a randomized algorithm correct with high probability. end-of-theorem

blocks.heading: Our Results
blocks.text: shows that, for APSP, as long as the goal is a truly subcubic running time, anything that can be achieved with integer-only tricks automatically applies to real-valued inputs as well

blocks.heading: Our Results
blocks.text: Naturally, the implication from is no longer as interesting as it was before the recent work of Alman and Vassilevska Williams [AlmanV26], which shows that both sides of this implication are unconditionally true. Nonetheless, we believe that the extensive techniques behind our proof of bring us closer to understanding the driving question of this paper about the limitations of integer-specific tricks in algorithm design

blocks.heading: Our Results
blocks.text: Alman and Vassilevska Williams [AlmanV26] propose that now, when we know that the original APSP Hypothesis is false, "one could refocus the hypotheses to be about combinatorial algorithms. " We remark that our reduction from is combinatorial (i. e., it does not use algebraic Strassenesque techniques common to fast matrix multiplication algorithms). Hence, we also establish that the "Combinatorial Real APSP Hypothesis" (asserting that no "combinatorial" algorithm for Real APSP runs in truly subcubic time in the real RAM model) implies the "Combinatorial Integer APSP Hypothesis" (asserting that no "combinatorial" algorithm for Integer APSP runs in truly subcubic time in the Word RAM model)

blocks.heading: Subcubic Real APSP
blocks.text: Curiously, in the real RAM model with multiplications (but even without flooring), there is an algorithm that solves Integer APSP in time n^(omega + o(1)) [Yuval76, ChanVX22], where omega < 3 denotes the matrix multiplication exponent. In combination with our real-to-integer reduction from, we hence get an algorithm solving Real APSP in truly subcubic time in this model

blocks.heading: Subcubic Real APSP
blocks.text: start-of-corollary: [Real APSP Hypothesis Is False in Real RAM Model with Multiplication] There exists a constant epsilon > 0, such that Real APSP can be solved in time O(n^(3-epsilon)) in the real RAM model with multiplications, by a randomized algorithm correct with high probability. end-of-corollary

blocks.heading: Subcubic Real APSP
blocks.text: We note that the recent independent work [AlmanV26], using a very different algorithm, establishes essentially the same theorem but in a more reasonable real RAM model with only comparison and addition (see Section for a discussion of computational models for reals)

blocks.heading: Exact Triangle.
blocks.text: APSP is known to be equivalent under subcubic reductions to the so-called Negative Triangle problem [VassilevskaW18], which asks, given an edge-weighted graph, if there exists a triangle (a cycle of length 3 ) with a negative total weight. A related problem, Exact Triangle is another central problem in fine-grained complexity. It asks if there is a triangle with total weight equal to zero. Negative Triangle (and hence also APSP) reduces to Exact Triangle [WilliamsW13], but there is no known reduction in the opposite direction; Exact Triangle seems to be a genuinely harder problem. Also for this problem we give a real-to-integer reduction:

blocks.heading: Exact Triangle.
blocks.text: start-of-theorem: [Real-to-Integer Reduction for Exact Triangle] If Integer Exact Triangle, with edge weights from (-u, dots, u), can be solved in time O(n^(3-epsilon)(log u)^(O(1))) for some constant epsilon > 0, then Real Exact Triangle can be solved in time O(n^(3-Omega(epsilon^2))), by a randomized algorithm correct with high probability. end-of-theorem

blocks.heading: Exact Triangle.
blocks.text: It is not a coincidence that we also prove this result; there is a technical reason why we get it along the way to. We elaborate on it in, but let us briefly explain this reason now: Our starting point is our previous real-to-integer reduction for the 3SUM problem [real3sum], the first such self-reduction in fine-grained complexity. To extend our 3SUM framework to APSP, we need to account for the two main differences between these two problems: first, 3SUM is an arithmetic/convolution problem while APSP is a graph/matrix problem; second, 3SUM is about equality constraints and APSP is about inequalities. The Exact Triangle problem is a graph/matrix problem about equality constraints, so it is a natural warm-up that lets us understand how to deal with the first difference without yet having to worry about the second one

blocks.heading: Computational Model
blocks.text: When working with real-valued inputs, one has to be careful about the choice of computational model. Obviously one cannot just work with the word RAM, which is the standard choice (for problems with integral inputs) in fine-grained complexity, because it lacks the ability to express real numbers. Its analog for reals, the real RAM model, quickly becomes unreasonably powerful if we allow for arbitrary arithmetic operations on infinite-precision numbers in constant time. For instance, flooring allows solving PSPACE-complete problems in polynomial time [HartmanisS74, Schonhage79]. Even without flooring, multiplication itself allows solving APSP with integer edge weights in the matrix multiplication time [Yuval76]. For our reductions to be meaningful, we want to state them in a model as weak as possible

blocks.heading: Computational Model
blocks.text: All our reductions work in the comparison-addition model, which is the word RAM model augmented with only two real-valued operations: comparisons and additions. Actually, they even work in the so-called realistic comparison-addition model [Section 1.1, real3sum], where the cost of evaluating a comparison of the form sum_i n_ialpha_i geq 0, where n_i 's are arbitrary non-zero integer coefficients and alpha_i 's are input reals, is smash(big(sum_i(1+log|n_i|)big)^(O(1))), and real addition can be performed only symbolically. A benefit of working with this model is that any algorithm for real-valued inputs can be efficiently simulated in the word RAM model on inputs that happen to be integral. In other words, trivial integer-to-real reductions do work with this model choice, and, combined with our real-to-integer reductions, they give fine-grained, subcubic equivalences of the real and integer variants of APSP and Exact Triangle. See [Section 1.1, real3sum] and [Appendix A in the full version, ChanVX22] for a deeper discussion of computational models for reals

blocks.heading: Open Problems
blocks.text: A natural direction for future research is to make our real-to-integer reduction more efficient. Ideally, one would like an O(n^(3-epsilon)) -time algorithm for Integer APSP to imply an tilde O(n^(3-epsilon)) -time algorithm for Real APSP, but already improving the savings from Omega(epsilon^3) to Omega(epsilon) would be interesting. Let us mention that, if one does not insist on the reduction being combinatorial, then it is already possible to improve Omega(epsilon^3) to Omega(epsilon^2) by using Matou s ek's fast algebraic dominance product algorithm [Matousek91] in the proof of

blocks.heading: Open Problems
blocks.text: In general, there are many fundamental problems for which the fastest known algorithms for reals are slower than what we can achieve with integer-specific techniques, e. g., linear programming [Dantzig65, Khachiyan79] or maximum flow [Orlin13, ChenKLPGS25]. Can we replace these techniques with more general ones, which also handle reals, possibly via real-to-integer reductions?

blocks.heading: Technical Overview
blocks.text: In this section we give a high-level overview of our results. They can be seen as a conceptual and technical extension of the real-to-integer framework from our earlier paper on the 3SUM problem [real3sum]. This extension concerns two orthogonal directions: from the arithmetic setting to graphs, and from equality constraints ( a + b = c ) to inequality constraints ( a + b leq c ). The transition from arithmetic to graph problems is technically tedious, but the transition from equalities to inequalities is the actual challenge. There are two concrete obstacles, namely two integer-specific tricks that need to be replaced with alternatives for reals (to be discussed soon), and overcoming them is the key technical contribution of our paper

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Framework
blocks.text: Before we can get to these new obstacles, it is instructive to understand the key ideas behind our earlier real-to-integer framework. For simplicity, focus on the 3SUM problem, which asks to detect whether a given set A contains a solution to the equation a + b + c = 0. In [real3sum], we show that this problem can be reduced from real-valued inputs to integer-valued inputs, in terms of subquadratic-time algorithms

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Framework
blocks.text: The starting point of that work is the Frank Tardos theorem from optimization, which can be stated as follows:

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Framework
blocks.text: start-of-theorem: [Frank Tardos [FrankT87] ] There is an algorithm that, given reals alpha in Real^d, runs in polynomial time d^(O(1)) and computes integers v in Int^d such that start-of-enumerate: [label=( )]. v _infty leq 2^(O(d^3)), and. alpha^T x geq 0 if and only if v^T x geq 0, for all x in -1, 0, 1 ^d. end-of-enumerate end-of-theorem

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Framework
blocks.text: Suppose we apply this theorem to the reals in our input set A = a_1, dots, a_n. Then the theorem supplies integers v_1, dots, v_n that can be directly used as substitutes for these reals; indeed, there is a real solution a_i + a_j + a_k = 0 if and only if there is an integer solution v_i + v_j + v_k = 0. While this is a fascinating starting point, the problem is that running the Frank Tardos theorem is too slow: the algorithm runs in polynomial time with some large exponent, and even if this exponent could be improved, it is unconditionally impossible to achieve subquadratic time. (For details, see [real3sum]. )

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Framework
blocks.text: Therefore, instead of applying the Frank Tardos theorem directly, [real3sum] proceeds differently. Here we describe this approach at a very high level, omitting many technical details without mentioning them. The approach can be summarized in the following steps: start-of-enumerate:. Rounding: Find an appropriate scale Delta in Realnneg and round all reals to integer multiples of Delta. Of course, we cannot actually round reals this operation is not supported in the real RAM model so we instead work with the usual weights but with pm Delta -approximate equalities. But, for simplicity, let us pretend in this overview that we can round. The scale Delta is chosen in such a way that the number of solutions after the rounding is close to the maximum n^2, say Theta(n^(2-epsilon)). This has an advantage and a disadvantage: the advantage is that we have introduced additive structure by rounding at this coarse-grained scale, and we will soon exploit that structure. The disadvantage is that we have introduced many false positive solutions, and in order to distinguish a true solution from these false positives, we are forced to list all rounded solutions.. Popular/unpopular decomposition: While the rounding has introduced a lot of additive structure globally, this does not mean that every item is affected by this structure locally. We therefore partition the elements into popular and unpopular ones, depending on their local additive structure. Concretely, we say that an element a_i is popular if it participates in many solutions of the form a_i + a_j = a_k + a_ell (after the rounding). The idea behind this decomposition is that the popular entries can be replaced by integers: via some involved additive combinatorics machinery, one can cover the popular entries by the subset sums of a set X of size at most d = n^(O(epsilon)) (a so-called subset sum cover ). Then we can apply the Frank Tardos theorem to X instead of A, which runs in time n^(O(epsilon)).. Listing rounded solutions: We now list all rounded solutions. Of course, replacing only the popular items by integers would not be fully sufficient, as in a solution a_i + a_j + a_k = 0 not all items need to be popular. We are left with three cases: start-of-itemize:. All-popular solutions: First, consider solutions a_i + a_j + a_k = 0 where all three items are popular. These can now be listed, by replacing popular reals with their integer representatives, and then using the integer algorithm (by basic tricks from fine-grained complexity, any detection algorithm can be turned into a listing algorithm). To keep this step efficient, we rely crucially on the guarantee from Step 1 that the number of rounded solutions is at most O(n^(2-epsilon)).. Partially popular solutions: Second, consider solutions a_i + a_j + a_k = 0 where some item is popular and some other item is unpopular. We cannot detect these solutions by a reduction to integers. Instead, we use a technical argument (a version of the "Fredman's trick meets dominance product" technique from [ChanVX23] ), exploiting both that solutions involving popular items can be efficiently listed (due to their structure), and that there are not many solutions involving unpopular items (due to their missing structure).. All-unpopular solutions: It remains to list solutions containing three unpopular items. To do so, we simply remove all popular items and iterate, starting over in Step 1. This is clearly correct, but not necessarily efficient, as we now have to worry about the number of iterations. In particular, if the number of iterations is n^epsilon then already listing the all-popular solutions across all iterations becomes too expensive. The insight is that, since there are many rounded solutions, at least Omega(n^(2-epsilon)), and since every unpopular item participates in few, a large fraction of items must be popular. We thus reduce the size of A considerably with each iteration, leading only to tilde O(n^(epsilon/2)) iterations in total. end-of-itemize end-of-enumerate

blocks.heading: APSP
blocks.text: Let us finally come back to APSP. A seminal result in fine-grained complexity is that APSP is equivalent (in terms of subcubic algorithms) to the Negative Triangle problem, asking whether a given tripartite graph contains a triangle (i, k, j) with a negative total edge weight, w(i, k) + w(k, j) + w(i, j) < 0. A closely related problem is Exact Triangle, where the goal is instead to decide if there is a triangle with the total weight equal to zero, w(i, k) + w(k, j) + w(i, j) = 0. That is, Exact Triangle can be seen as a variant of 3SUM where the items have to be placed on the edges of a triangle, and Negative Triangle can be seen as the variant with " < " instead of " = "

blocks.heading: APSP
blocks.text: An adaptation of the real-to-integer reduction should therefore be implemented in two steps: (1) from 3SUM to Exact Triangle, i. e., from an arithmetic to a graph problem, and (2) from Exact Triangle to Negative Triangle, i. e., from " = " to " < ". These two steps yield separate challenges. The first one is simpler; at least conceptually, the approach from before can work (though there are technical issues). The second one is much more challenging, and in the following overview we only focus on the two concrete obstacles that need to be overcome

blocks.heading: Problem 1: Additive Hashing.
blocks.text: We start with the bigger of the two problems. An important aspect of the real-to-integer framework that we have not highlighted before is the following: the integers resulting from the Frank Tardos theorem are huge! Even when applied in the elaborate way described above, through additive combinatorics and subset sum covers, we call the Frank Tardos theorem with d = n^(epsilon) and thus the resulting integers have magnitude exp(d^(O(1))) = exp(n^(O(epsilon))). In particular, performing any arithmetic operation on these numbers takes time n^(O(epsilon)). We can certainly not afford to lose this extra factor in the running time, since the saving in the aforementioned reduction is less than n^(epsilon/2)

blocks.heading: Problem 1: Additive Hashing.
blocks.text: For this reason, an important intermediate step, after we have applied Frank Tardos but before we list integer solutions, is to reduce the size of these integers; in other words, we perform a universe reduction. For 3SUM this is simple: all we need is a hash function h that maps arbitrarily large integers to a small universe, say set(-n^(O(1)), dots, n^(O(1))), and that is additive in the sense that a + b + c = 0 if and only if h(a) + h(b) + h(c) = 0 (with good probability). Many families of additive hash functions are known, e. g., h(x) = x bmod p for a randomly chosen prime p (and then working with equality modulo p )

blocks.heading: Problem 1: Additive Hashing.
blocks.text: If we want to apply the same approach for Negative Triangle, we would need a hash function satisfying the analogous property that a + b + c < 0 if and only if h(a) + h(b) + h(c) < 0 (with good probability). However, such a hash function to a small universe cannot exist! This forces us to take a different route which, we believe, is of independent conceptual interest

blocks.heading: Solution 1: Doubling Reduction
blocks.text: As we are looking for a universe reduction for Negative Triangle (i. e., APSP) from exponential to polynomial weights, perhaps a natural starting point is Fischer's recent universe reduction from polynomially-bounded to linear weights [Fischer26]. Let us take a step back to describe some ideas behind that work. Instead of directly using a hash function to reduce the universe size, it suggests a detour in three steps: (i) first, round the integers so that the set of weights A = w(i, j): i, j in [n] admits some weak structure, (ii) then amplify this weak structure into much stronger structure called low doubling, (iii) and only then hash the weights to a small universe. Steps (i) and (iii) are similar to our setup here, but the crucial step is to apply the doubling reduction in between. Intuitively, when the weights are structured in this sense we circumvent the counterexamples showing that the desired hash functions cannot exist in general. To define low doubling for an integer set A, let A + A = a + b: a, b in A denote its sumset. The doubling is defined as the ratio K: = |A + A| / |A|. Fischer's doubling reduction essentially allows for the following trade-off: the weights can be transformed to have arbitrarily small doubling K, at the cost of an overhead of O(n^3 / K^(Omega(1))) in the running time. In particular, K can be an arbitrarily small polynomial

blocks.heading: Solution 1: Doubling Reduction
blocks.text: Unfortunately, the doubling reduction is long and involved. It consists of five steps, four of which need to be reproved for our setting of approximate reals (recall that we always work with reals represented up to pm Delta ). In we work through these four steps, and along the way also reprove a version of the famous Balog Szemerédi Gowers (BSG) theorem for approximate reals. But with the doubling reduction in place, we can repair the approach from before as follows. We replace the second step of the real-to-integer framework (Section ) with the following more elaborate version: start-of-enumerate:. Decompose the weights into popular and unpopular ones. Our goal in the following steps is to replace the popular ones by small integers.. Run the doubling reduction on the popular weights. This allows us to assume that the popular weights have doubling K = n^delta for some arbitrarily small delta. It still remains to replace them by small integers.. Apply Freiman's theorem from additive combinatorics to obtain a small subset sum cover X of the popular weights. One can achieve that X has size d = |X| leq (K log |A|)^(O(1)) = n^(O(delta)). Then use the Frank Tardos theorem, applied to X, to replace the popular weights by integers of size exp(d^(O(1))) = exp(n^(O(delta))). end-of-enumerate Thus, the resulting integers are still exponentially large, and performing operations on them takes time n^(O(delta)). However, the new freedom, due to the doubling reduction, is that we can pick delta arbitrarily small, independent of the other parameters of the reduction. In particular, when setting delta sufficiently small in terms of epsilon we can make sure that the total overhead due to the large weights becomes, say, O(n^(epsilon/4)), and so the real-to-integer reduction stays efficient. This resolves the first problem. There are two remaining technical issues worth commenting on. First, if Step 2. 2 runs in time O(n^3 / K^(Omega(1))) = O(n^(3-Omega(delta))), and we repeat this step over the tilde O(n^(epsilon/2)) iterations, why does this not cancel all of our improvements, given that delta is chosen to be much smaller than epsilon? The insight is that every popular edge appears in the doubling reduction in at most one iteration. Thus, analyzing the O(n^3 / K^(Omega(1))) running time in terms of the number of edges rather than vertices shows that the total time remains subcubic

blocks.heading: Solution 1: Doubling Reduction
blocks.text: Second, how can we implement Freiman's theorem from additive combinatorics? This problem has been considered by Randolph and W e grzycki [RandolphW24]; however, their algorithm has an FPT-dependence on the doubling K which is prohibitively slow for us. Luckily, as a side product of our earlier work [real3sum], we already have a weaker "Poor Man's" version of the theorem which can be implemented sufficiently fast

blocks.heading: Problem 2: Scaling
blocks.text: The second problem concerns the standard "scaling trick" that is used to reduce from Negative Triangle to Exact Triangle, i. e., from " < " to " = " constraints. More specifically, this trick allows us to reduce the Negative Triangle problem to few instances of Exact Triangle, where each instance is promised to only contain nonnegative triangles. It essentially works by determining the weight of the most negative triangle bit-by-bit. However, for infinite-precision reals, such a bit trick clearly cannot work. The same problem has occurred in [ChanVX22], where the goal was to reduce from APSP via Exact Triangle to the All-Edges Sparse Triangle problem; their solution was to circumvent the detour via Exact Triangle altogether. Unfortunately, this is not an option for us

blocks.heading: Problem 2: Scaling
blocks.text: Concretely in our setting, the scaling trick is still necessary for many technical arguments under the hood. For instance, the doubling reduction is built on various heavy/light tricks, which reduce some weights to have low doubling, but for other weights they simply enumerate all zero-weight triangles involving these weights. Hence, without the scaling trick we could potentially miss some negative triangles

blocks.heading: Solution 2: Fredman's Trick meets Dominance Product
blocks.text: Our solution is as follows. Suppose that we still follow our framework from before; in each iteration, which negative triangles do we miss? We can ignore triangles consisting of only unpopular edges as they will be dealt with in future iterations, so only focus on triangles involving at least some popular edge. If such a triangle is just barely negative in the sense that -Delta < w(i, k) + w(k, j) + w(i, j) < 0, then the rounding will actually turn this triangle into a zero-weight triangle, and therefore our real-to-integer reduction will correctly take care of it. This only leaves the very negative triangles of weight less than -Delta. To deal with these, we follow the "Fredman's trick meets dominance product" technique due to Chan, Vassilevska W., and Xu [ChanVX23], developed as a follow-up to [ChanVX22]. The idea is roughly as follows. Each popular edge, say (i, j), is part of many zero-weight triangles. Thus, when sampling a vertex k', with good probability we have that w(i, j) = -w(i, k') - w(k', j). Then, the condition that (i, k, j) is a negative triangle can be expressed as 0 > w(i, k) + w(k, j) + w(i, j) = w(i, k) + w(k, j) - w(i, k') - w(k', j), or, equivalently, w(i, k') - w(i, k) > w(k, j) - w(k', j). This elementary rearrangement is sometimes called "Fredman's trick" [Fredman]. Note that the left-hand side only depends on i and k and the right-hand side only depends on k and j (assuming that k' is fixed). The problem of detecting a negative triangle therefore reduces to deciding if there is a triangle (i, k, j) in a tripartite graph, where the edge weight in one prescribed edge part is larger than that in another edge part. This is an instance of the so-called dominance product problem, which is known to be computable in subcubic time O(n^((omega+3)/2)) [Matousek91]. In this way, detecting the very negative triangle only leads to an overall subcubic overhead

blocks.heading: Problems
blocks.text: Using a standard chain of reductions [VassilevskaW18], it is well-known that the existence of an algorithm in truly subcubic time for Integer APSP is equivalent to the existence of an algorithm in truly subcubic time for Integer Negative Triangle. In the same paper, Vassilevska Williams and Williams give another reduction from APSP to Negative Triangle that avoids a binary search on the space of possible triangle weights and hence also works for real numbers. Therefore, also Real APSP and Real Negative Triangle are subcubically equivalent. In all our reductions we exclusively work with Negative Triangle instead of APSP

blocks.text: For the integer variants we throughout assume that the weights are from the universe -u, dots, u. Throughout the paper we also allow integer and real instances of any of the defined problem to contain missing values replaced by a dummy symbol bot. To simplify notation, we use suitable conventions such as x + bot = bot for x in Real or bot not < 0, wherever necessary. Entries equal to bot could also be simulated by sufficiently large numbers

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Toolbox
blocks.text: In this section, we develop and recap some necessary tools for real-to-integer reductions as well as APSP in general. We start with some preliminary definitions concerning rounded reals and select-plus rank ( ). Next, we state the edge weight reduction for APSP that we use, in the spirit of a universe reduction ( ). Then, we recap our real-to-integer reduction tools and prove the precise primitive used for Exact Triangle and APSP ( ). Finally, we state listing-to-decision reductions ( )

blocks.heading: Approximate Reals
blocks.text: Morally, our algorithm works by rounding real numbers to an appropriate scale to create structure and then uses that structure. However, the restricted Real RAM model does not allow for a rounding operation, since that would already allow for unreasonably efficient algorithms (e. g., [HartmanisS74, Schonhage79] ). Nonetheless, we can carry out the rounding symbolically. The operation we would like to be able to perform is rounding a real x in Real to its nearest integer multiple of some scale Delta in Real. Instead, we can keep track of x and Delta separately, and whenever we perform a comparison lceil x / Delta rfloor = lceil y / Delta rfloor of two reals x, y in Real that should be rounded, we instead check that x in [y-Delta, y + Delta] (via two comparisons x ge y-Delta and x le y + Delta ). Note that this is not exactly the same operation as comparing rounded numbers, but performs a similar role in the sense that it allows us to compare numbers on a coarser scale

blocks.heading: Approximate Reals
blocks.text: We write x = y pm Delta to denote x in [y-Delta, y+Delta]. For two sets X, C subseteq Real, we say that C is a Delta -cover of X if X subseteq bigcup_(c in C)[c-Delta, c+Delta]. In other words, for every x in X there should be a c in C with x = c pm Delta. For Deltage0, a set X subseteq Real is Delta -spaced if |x - x'| ge Delta for every pair of distinct elements x, x'in X

blocks.heading: Approximate Reals
blocks.text: We denote by X the size of a minimum Delta -cover of X. Note that such a minimum Delta -cover of size X is easy to compute in time O( X log X ) by a simple greedy algorithm: Indeed, just sort X and sweep over its elements in increasing order. For every encountered and currently uncovered number x in X, we add x + Delta to the Delta -cover and skip all numbers less than or equal to x + 2Delta

blocks.heading: Select-Plus Rank for Approximate Reals
blocks.text: For Delta in Realnneg, the Delta -approximate select-plus rank (or just Delta -approximate rank ) of a matrix A in (Real cup bot )^(ntimes n) is the smallest integer r ge 0 such that there are matrices U in Real^(ntimes r) and V in Real^(r times n) satisfying the following: For all (i, j) in [n]^2 with A[i,j] ne bot there is a k in [r] such that: A[i,j] = U[i,k] + V[k, j] pm Delta. When S in ([r] cup bot )^(ntimes n) is a matrix such that S[i,j] = k, we call (U, V, S) a Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition of A. Whenever we say that a matrix A has Delta -approximate rank at most r, we assume that we also have access to a Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition of A

blocks.heading: Select-Plus Rank for Approximate Reals
blocks.text: We first observe that the Delta -approximate rank of a matrix is not very sensitive to the choice of Delta, i. e., when we scale Delta by a constant factor, the rank also only changes by a constant factor

blocks.heading: Select-Plus Rank for Approximate Reals
blocks.text: start-of-proof: Let (U, V, S) be the Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition of A. To construct a Delta/c -approximate rank- (2c+1)r decomposition, simply replace each U[i,k] with 2c+1 entries U[i,k]-cDelta/(2c), dots, U[i,k] + cDelta/(2c). Do the same for V and replace V[k,j] with entries V[k,j]-cDelta/(2c), dots, V[k,j] + cDelta/(2c). Finally, update S by finding the correct new entry among the 2c+1 newly created entries. This also dominates the running time. end-of-proof

blocks.heading: Potential-Adjusting Reductions and Edge Weight Reduction
blocks.text: To make it easier to keep track of how our reductions manipulate the graph and the number of triangles of certain weights, we reuse the definition of a potential-adjusting reduction, defined in [Fischer26]. Informally, a potential-adjusting reduction is a reduction that allows us to delete edges and to add node weights in a way such that all triangles of weight 0 (up to pm Delta in our case) are kept track of. Moreover, every triangle that survives the reduction will keep its weight (the value of A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] ) unchanged. We use the following two definitions

blocks.heading: Potential-Adjusting Reductions and Edge Weight Reduction
blocks.text: start-of-definition: [Potential Adjustment] Let (A, B, C), (A', B', C') be instances of Real Exact Triangle of the same size n. We say that (A', B', C') is a potential adjustment of (A, B, C) if there are potential functions u, v, w in Real^n such that: (r@( )r@(quad)r@(quad)r@( )r@(quad)l@( )l) A'[i,k] =& A[i,k]-u[i]+v[k] &text(or)& A'[i,k]=&perp &text(for all )(i, k)&in[n]^2, [1.5mm] B'[k,j] =& B[k,j]-v[k]+w[j] &text(or)& B'[k,j]=&perp &text(for all )(k, j)&in[n]^2, [1.5mm] C'[i,j] =& C[i,j]+u[i]-w[j] &text(or)& C'[i,j]=&perp &text(for all )(i, j)&in[n]^2. end-of-definition

blocks.heading: Potential-Adjusting Reductions and Edge Weight Reduction
blocks.text: start-of-definition: [ Delta -Approximate Potential-Adjusting Reduction] A Delta -approximate potential-adjusting reduction in time T is an algorithm that runs in time T and takes as input a parameter Delta in Realnneg as well as a Real Exact Triangle instance (A, B, C) of size n and outputs a pair ( I, T) where start-of-itemize:. I is a set of potential adjustments of (A, B, C), and. T subseteq [n]^3 is a set of triples of size T le T, end-of-itemize such that each Delta -approximate triangle (i, k, j) in (A, B, C) appears in T or as a Delta -approximate triangle in an instance in I. end-of-definition

blocks.text: We use the following edge weight reduction to an approximately uniform and approximately low doubling weight set for matrices of bounded approximate rank. The statement (and reduction chain in the proof) mostly mirrors its exact version in [Fischer26] (some of which already mirror reductions from [AbboudFJVX25] in a rectangular setting). Our approach inherently only works for the corresponding Delta -approximate definitions, which means we have to reprove the weight reduction for this setting. This is mostly a tedious but natural transfer to corresponding approximate versions of each argument in the chain. The proof of can be found in. blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: In this subsection, we first list the necessary real-to-integer toolbox, which we reuse from [real3sum]

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: start-of-definition: [Subset Sum Cover] Let A subseteq Real. A pair (alpha, f), where alpha in Real^d and f: A to 0, 1 ^d, is called a Delta -approximate subset sum cover of A if it satisfies a = alpha^T f(a) pm Delta for each a in A. We call d the rank of the subset sum cover. end-of-definition

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: start-of-theorem: [Poor Man's Freiman's Theorem [Theorem 3.10, real3sum] ] Let Delta in Realnneg, K ge 1, and let A subseteq Real be a set satisfying the Delta -approximate doubling condition A+A le Kcabs A. Then there is a Delta -approximate subset sum cover of A with rank (K log|A|)^(O(1)). It can be computed in time tilde O(|A|^2). end-of-theorem

blocks.text: The next lemma is also already proven in [real3sum], except for the third property. Since the hash function in the proof is monotone except for a random offset independent of the function argument, property (iii) follows immediately from property (ii). The proof internally uses the Frank Tardos theorem [FrankT87]

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Hashing Reals to Integers [Lemma 3.9, real3sum] ] Let Delta in Realnneg and let A subseteq Real be a set with a Delta -approximate subset sum cover of rank (Klog |A|)^(O(1)). There is a randomized algorithm that runs in time tilde O(|A| + (Klog|A|)^(O(1))) and computes a function h: A to [pm 2^((Klog |A|)^(O(1)))] such that: start-of-enumerate: [label=( )]. For all a, b, c in A with a + b + c = 0 pm Delta, we have Pr[h(a) + h(b) + h(c) = 0] geq Omega(1).. For all a, b, c in A with h(a) + h(b) + h(c) = 0, we have a + b + c = 0 pm 100 Delta.. For all a, b, c in A with h(a) + h(b) + h(c) < 0, we have a+b+c < 100Delta. end-of-enumerate end-of-lemma

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: The next lemma is the main goal of this subsection. It combines the previously cited tools and is the single way in which we use them in the main proof. The lemma shows that if at least one input matrix has low Delta -approximate rank, we can convert the edge weights to integers

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals] Let Delta in Realnneg, let s ge 1 be a parameter, and let A, B, C in (Real cup bot )^(ntimes n) such that: start-of-enumerate:. at least one of A, B, and C has Delta -approximate rank at most r, and. the number of 2Delta -approximate exact triangles in (A, B, C) is at most T. end-of-enumerate Then there is an algorithm that reports a set of triangles T, and outputs sn^(o(1)) triples of integer matrices X, Y, Z in ([pm 2^((s log r)^(O(1)))] cup bot )^(n times n) such that: start-of-enumerate: [label=( )]. | T| leq T, and the number of exact triangles in any (X, Y, Z) is at most T,. any Delta -approximate exact triangle in (A, B, C) is in T or an exact triangle in some (X, Y, Z),. any negative triangle (i, k, j) in some instance (X, Y, Z) satisfies A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] < 2Delta. end-of-enumerate The reduction runs in time ens*( (rs)^(O(1))n^2 + n^3 (s^(1/10^5)))^(1+o(1)). end-of-lemma

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: proof Assume that we are given a Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition of C, otherwise exchange the matrices appropriately. First, we use to turn it into a Delta' -approximate rank decomposition of rank r' coloneqq 1001r for Delta' coloneqq Delta/500. Initialize Tcoloneqqemptyset. For each shift sigma in Delta' cdot -500, -499, ldots, 500, run the following steps on (A, B, C_sigma), where C_sigma[i, j] = C[i, j] - sigma for non- bot entries. Subtracting sigma appropriately in the low-rank decomposition gives a Delta' -approximate rank- r' decomposition of C_sigma. Then apply the edge weight reduction to approximately uniform and small doubling weights ( ) at scale Delta' to (A, B, C_sigma). This returns a pair ( I, T_sigma) of I le sn^(o(1)) potential-adjusted instances and some exceptional triangles T_sigma. Insert into T every triangle (i, k, j) in T_sigma whose original weight satisfies A[i, k] + B[k, j] + C[i, j] = 0 pm Delta. Next, we process the instances (hat A, hat B, hat C) in I. Let X subseteq Real denote the set of entries in the three matrices hat A, hat B, hat C. This set satisfies |X|_(pm Delta') le r' and |X+X|_(pmDelta') le s |X|_(pmDelta'). Compute the greedy minimum Delta' -cover Y of X, of size |Y|=|X|_(pmDelta')le r' (with ) and for x in X write f(x) for the unique y in Y with x = y pm Delta'. The greedy construction gives Ysubseteq X+Delta' and places its centers more than 2Delta' apart. Thus |Y|_(pmDelta')=|Y|, and therefore |Y+Y|_(pmDelta')le |X+X|_(pmDelta')le s|X|_(pmDelta')=s|Y|_(pmDelta'). Apply Poor Man's Freiman's theorem to Y to compute a Delta' -approximate subset sum cover of rank (slog r')^(O(1)), which is also a 4Delta' -approximate subset sum cover

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Low-Rank Reals
blocks.text: For g = 1, dots, O(log n), perform the following steps: Hash the reals in Y to integers with at scale 4Delta', and let h_g: Y to [pm 2^((slog r)^(O(1)))] denote the resulting hash function. Replace all occurrences in hat A, hat B, and hat C of a real xin Real with the integer h_g(f(x)), and add the resulting integer instance to the output. In the end, return T together with the integer instances

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: Consider a Delta -approximate exact triangle in the original instance with weight w: = A[i, k] + B[k, j] + C[i, j]. Focus on the shift sigma satisfying |w - sigma| le Delta'. For this shift, the triangle is either in T_sigma, in which case it is added to T, or it satisfies hat A[i,k] + hat B[k,j] + hat C[i,j] = 0 pmDelta' for at least one instance (hat A, hat B, hat C) in I by the guarantee of the Delta' -approximate potential-adjusting reduction. Then f(hat A[i,k]) + f(hat B[k,j]) + f(hat C[i,j]) = 0 pm 4Delta', since f(x) = x pm Delta' for all x in X. For any g, it also satisfies h_g(f(hat A[i,k])) + h_g(f(hat B[k,j])) + h_g(f(hat C[i,j])) = 0 with constant probability by, property (i), making (i, k, j) an exact integer triangle in the reduced instance. After O(log n) independent repetitions, a union bound over the at most n^3 triangles shows that every Delta -approximate exact triangle outside T appears as an exact triangle in at least one integer instance with high probability, proving property (ii)

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: We also need to argue that we do not get too many integer exact triangles, that is, property (i). First, every triangle in T is Delta -approximate in the original instance, so | T|le T. Next, use property (ii) of the real-to-integer hash function ( ), which states that any integer triangle with h_g(f(hat A[i,k])) + h_g(f(hat B[k,j])) + h_g(f(hat C[i,j])) = 0, for some g, also satisfies f(hat A[i,k]) + f(hat B[k,j]) + f(hat C[i,j]) = 0 pm 400Delta'. Since f(x) = x pm Delta' for all x in X, we must also have hat A[i,k] + hat B[k,j] + hat C[i,j] = 0 pm 500Delta'. Potential adjustments preserve this triangle weight; undoing the shift only adds sigma. Thus the original weight has magnitude at most |sigma| + 500Delta' le 2Delta. There are at most T such triangles

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: We prove the third property about negative triangles in a similar way. Consider (i, k, j) and some g such that h_g(f(hat A[i,k])) + h_g(f(hat B[k,j])) + h_g(f(hat C[i,j])) < 0. Then hat A[i,k] + hat B[k,j] + hat C[i,j] < 500Delta', so the original weight is less than sigma+500Delta'le2Delta, proving property (iii)

blocks.heading: Running Time.
blocks.text: The edge weight reduction ( ) runs in time (rsn^2 + n^3/s^(1/10^5))^(1+o(1)) per shift, which also bounds the number of exceptional triangles that we enumerate. Computing Y and the map f takes time tilde O(n^2) per instance. Poor Man's Freiman's theorem ( ) takes time tilde O(r^2) per instance. Finally, hashing each instance to integers ( ) takes time tilde O(r + (slog r)^(O(1))) per instance. There are O(1) shifts and we repeat O(log n) times. In total, the running time becomes ens*( (rs)^(O(1))n^2 + frac(n^3)(s^(1/10^5)) )^(1+o(1)), as claimed. proof

blocks.text: We use the following standard listing-to-decision reductions for the triangle problems of interest, Exact Triangle and Negative Triangle, due to Vassilevska Williams and Williams [VassilevskaW18]. They show that an algorithm that solves the problem in subcubic time can also be used to list a subcubic number of solutions in subcubic time

blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Listing-to-Decision for Integer Exact Triangle, [VassilevskaW18] ] If Integer Exact Triangle can be decided in time O(n^(3-epsilon) (log u)^(O(1))) for some constant epsilon > 0, then one can also list up to T solutions in time O(n^(3 - epsilon) T^(epsilon/3) (log u)^(O(1))). end-of-lemma

blocks.heading: Listing-to-Decision Reductions for Triangle Problems
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Listing-to-Decision for Integer Negative Triangle, [VassilevskaW18] ] If Integer Negative Triangle can be decided in time O(n^(3-epsilon) (log u)^(O(1))) for some constant epsilon > 0, then one can also list up to T solutions in time O(n^(3 - epsilon) T^(epsilon/3) (log u)^(O(1))). end-of-lemma

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for Exact Triangle
blocks.text: In this section we prove and develop almost all remaining parts to prove our real-to-integer reduction for APSP ( )

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: The initial setup of the algorithm is more or less exactly the same as for 3SUM [real3sum]; the adaptations to triangles instead of 3SUM solutions are mainly concerned with the different number of possible solutions

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: We call a triple (i, k, j) in [n]^3 a Delta -approximate triangle (or Delta -approximate solution ) if A[i, k] + B[k, j] + C[i,j] = 0 pm Delta

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Approximation Threshold] Let A, B, C in (Real cup bot )^(ntimes n) be matrices and let K ge 1. There is a randomized algorithm that runs in time K(log n)^(O(1)) and either detects an Exact Triangle solution (in which case there are at least Omega(n^3/K) exact solutions), decides that the number of infty -approximate solutions is at most O(n^3/K), or computes a threshold Delta in Real_(ge 0) such that: start-of-enumerate: [label=( )]. the number of Delta -approximate solutions is at most O(n^3 / K), and. the number of 2Delta -approximate solutions is at least Omega(n^3 / K). end-of-enumerate end-of-lemma start-of-proof: Consider a sequence of length n^3 of numbers equal to the absolute weight of all triangles |A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j]| for all triples i, k, j in [n], sorted in increasing order (where bot -values are considered the largest values). We aim to find one triple (i^*, k^*, j^*) whose rank in this sorted order is between n^3/K and 2n^3/K. After having found such a triple we can return one of the three possible answers: If A[i^*,k^*] + B[k^*, j^*] + C[i^*,j^*] = 0, we have found an Exact Triangle solution. In this case, the rank of the selected triple also guarantees at least n^3/K exact solutions. If one of A[i^*,k^*], B[k^*, j^*], and C[i^*,j^*] equals bot, then so does their sum and we can conclude that the number of infty -approximate solutions is at most 2n^3/K. If none of these cases apply, we set 2Delta coloneqq |A[i^*,k^*] + B[k^*, j^*] + C[i^*,j^*]|. Since the rank of (i^*, k^*, j^*) is at least n^3/K, there must be at least n^3/K triples (i, k, j) with |A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j]| le |A[i^*,k^*] + B[k^*, j^*] + C[i^*,j^*]| = 2Delta. All of these triples form 2Delta -approximate solutions. On the other hand, there are at most 2n^3/K triples (i, k, j) with |A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j]| < |A[i^*,k^*] + B[k^*, j^*] + C[i^*,j^*]| = 2Delta, and only those triples can form Delta -approximate solutions since Delta > 0. To find (i^*, k^*, j^*) we apply a sketching technique. Let R coloneqq Theta(log n) and sample R K triples (i, k, j) in [n]^3 uniformly at random. Among them, pick the one for which |A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j]| is 1. 5R -th smallest. Equivalently, we choose R K uniformly random positions in the sorted order, and commit to the 1. 5R -th smallest position among the samples. For each sample, the probability that it has rank below n^3 / K is exactly 1/K. Therefore, the expected number of samples below this rank is R K / K = R. By Chernoff's bound it follows that with high probability there are fewer than 1. 5R samples below rank n^3 / K and the lower bound on the 2Delta -approximate solutions follows. Similarly, the expected number of samples below rank 2n^3 / K is 2R, and by Chernoff's bound with high probability there are at least 1. 5R such samples. Thus, the upper bound on the Delta -approximate solutions holds too. end-of-proof

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Popular/Unpopular Decomposition] Let A, B, C in (Real cup bot )^(ntimes n) be matrices, Delta in Realnneg, and let L ge 1. There is a randomized algorithm that runs in time tilde O(n^2L^2) and partitions the edge set into popular and unpopular edges such that: start-of-enumerate: [label=( )]. Each popular edge is in at least n/L 2Delta -approximate solutions.. There are at most 6n^3/L 2Delta -approximate solutions involving unpopular edges. end-of-enumerate end-of-lemma start-of-proof: We first describe a simple deterministic but slow solution: Initially, treat every edge as popular. For each edge that is contained in fewer than n/L 2Delta -approximate solutions, we mark it as unpopular. After this process ends, the first property holds by construction. By definition, each unpopular edge is involved in at most n/L 2Delta -approximate solutions. Summing over all 3n^2 edges proves property (ii). Since we cannot afford to compute the number of triangles exactly, we implement the above idea with estimated counts. For each C -edge (i, j) in [n]^2, sample Theta(L^2 log n) uniformly random values k in [n] and count how many such triples form a 2Delta -approximate solution (i, k, j). ( A and B are symmetric. ) We can then simply scale the sample count to get an additive approximation of the number of solutions involving this edge within error n/2L. Chernoff's bound shows that the approximation works with high probability. Now simply use the estimated counts to run the above described algorithm but mark an edge as unpopular if its estimated number of 2Delta -approximate solutions is less than the threshold tau coloneqq 3n/2L. After the algorithm, each popular edge is still in at least tau -n/2L = n/L 2Delta -approximate solutions. Summing over all edges shows that the number of 2Delta -approximate solutions involving unpopular edges is at most 3n^2 cdot ens*(tau + frac(n)(2L)) = 3n^2 cdot frac(2n)(L) = frac(6n^3)(L). qedhere end-of-proof

blocks.text: Now, we are left with only 3 types of solutions: start-of-enumerate:. Solutions with only popular edges,. solutions with at least one popular edge and at least one unpopular edge, and. solutions with only unpopular edges. end-of-enumerate We show how to detect any solutions of types 1 and 2 in respectively. In, we show how to deal with solutions of type 3 and complete the proof of

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: Combining the lower bound on the number of 2Delta -approximate solutions from the choice of Delta ( ) and the upper bound on the number of 2Delta -approximate solutions involving unpopular elements, we can observe the following

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: Recall the definition of the Delta -approximate rank of a matrix. We prove that after applying our decomposition into popular and unpopular edges, the popular edges must have low rank

blocks.heading: Popular/Unpopular Decomposition
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Popular Instances Have Low Rank] Let Delta in Realnneg, Lge 1, and A, B, C in (Real cup bot )^(ntimes n) be matrices where each C -edge (i, j) with C[i,j] ne bot is in at least n/L Delta -approximate solutions. Then, we can compute a Delta -approximate rank- O(Llog n) decomposition of C in time O(Ln^2log n). end-of-lemma proof Initialize the Delta -approximate rank- O(L log n) decomposition (U, V, S) such that U and V contain only 0 and S contains only bot entries. The algorithm runs in Theta(L log n) iterations. In an iteration g, we sample k in [n] uniformly at random. Now, for any (i, j) in [n]^2 such that (i, k, j) is a Delta -approximate solution, we set U[i, g] coloneqq -A[i,k], quad V[g,j] coloneqq -B[k,j], quad text(and ) S[i,j] coloneqq g. Finally, we return (U, V, S) as our decomposition

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: Suppose k is sampled in iteration g. For all i, j for which (i, k, j) is a Delta -approximate solution, that is, A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] = 0 pm Delta, we have U[i,g] + V[g,j] = -A[i,k] - B[k,j] = C[i,j] pm Delta. Therefore, S[i,j] is assigned correctly. It remains to show that after Theta(L log n) iterations, every S[i,j] was assigned at least once. Since every (i, j) is in at least n/L Delta -approximate solutions, every iteration assigns S[i,j] with probability at least 1/L. Hence after O(Llog n) iterations, every (i, j) was assigned at least once with high probability and we return a correct Delta -approximate rank- O(Llog n) decomposition of C

blocks.heading: Running Time.
blocks.text: Each iteration can easily be implemented in time O(n^2). The running time therefore follows from the number of iterations. proof

blocks.heading: Type 1: Only Popular Edges
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Type-1 Solutions] Assume Integer Exact Triangle is in time O(n^(3-epsilon) (log u)^(O(1))). Then there is an algorithm that detects any solution with only popular edges in time ens*( n^2(KL)^(O(1)) + frac(|P|n^(1+o(1)))(K^(Omega(epsilon))) )^(1+o(1)). end-of-lemma proof First set the unpopular entries of C to bot, keeping A and B unchanged. By the definition of P ( ) and, we can compute a 2Delta -approximate rank- O(Llog n) decomposition for C, which we can easily turn into a Delta/2 -approximate rank- O(Llog n) decomposition with. Now also set the unpopular entries of A and B to bot. There are only |P| edges left

blocks.heading: Type 1: Only Popular Edges
blocks.text: We apply a standard high degree/low degree split. For some parameter M to be determined later, call a node v light if deg(v) le M and heavy otherwise. We enumerate all triangles involving at least one light node by iterating over all light nodes v and all pairs of adjacent edges. blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for APSP
blocks.text: For Real APSP, at first glance it seems hard to generalize the approach from to negative triangles since the threshold choice Delta and popularity only bound the number of triangles summing to 0 up to pm Delta; the number of negative triangles is unbounded. However, there is a simple fix that allows us to reuse basically the full previous reduction. Namely, if there exists a very negative triangle, that is, a triple (i, k, j) satisfying A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] < -Delta, in an instance of sufficiently low approximate rank, then a negative triangle is simple to detect. Indeed, we can afford to iterate over the inner dimension of the approximate-rank decomposition and can then find a negative triangle using Fredman's trick and dominance product in truly subcubic time. The next lemma formalizes this idea. This step allows us to assume in the following that every negative triangle must also be a Delta -approximate exact triangle. Therefore, all other steps from apply

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for APSP
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Detecting Very Negative Triangles In Low-Rank Instances] Assume that Integer APSP is in time O(n^(3-epsilon)(log u)^(O(1))). Let Delta in Real_(geq 0), and let (A, B, C) be a Real Negative Triangle instance, along with a Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition of C. There is an algorithm running in time tilde O(rn^(3-epsilon)) that either outputs a negative triangle in (A, B, C) or reports that every triangle has weight at least -Delta. end-of-lemma proof Take the given Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition (U, V, S) of C, and use to turn it into a Delta/2 -approximate rank- 5r -decomposition. For all ell in [5r], define A_ell[i,k] &coloneqq mathmakebox[4cm][l](A[i,k] + U[i,ell]) & text(if A[i,k] ne bot, ) bot &text(otherwise; ) B_ell[k,j] &coloneqq mathmakebox[4cm][l](-B[k,j] - V[ell,j] - Delta/2)& text(if B[k,j] ne bot, ) bot &text(otherwise. ) We aim to compute a dominance product defined by D_ell[i,j] coloneqq 1 &text(if exists k in [n]: A_ell[i,k] < B_ell[k,j], ) 0 & text(otherwise. ) Once we have computed D_ell, we check if there are (i, j) such that S[i,j] = ell and D_ell[i,j] =1, and find a witness k for the dominance product in linear time. Then, we output the triangle (i, k, j) and stop the algorithm. If no witness is found for any ell, we report that every triangle has weight at least -Delta

blocks.heading: Real-to-Integer Reduction for APSP
blocks.text: To compute D_ell, we use the fast algorithm for Integer APSP: First, since computing D_ell by definition requires only comparisons of matrix entries, we can simply replace all real entries by integers (by sorting all entries in A_ell and B_ell and assigning integers in a way that keeps the order). Then, negate the entries in B_ell to compute the integer min-plus product M_ell[i,j] coloneqq min_(k in [n]) A_ell[i,k] - B_ell[k,j]. Finally, the dominance product outputs can be inferred by setting D_ell[i,j] = 1 if and only if M_ell[i,j] < 0. (Of course, we may also compute each dominance product unconditionally in time O(n^((3+omega)/2)) using Matou s ek's algorithm [Matousek91]; however, we prefer our conditional statement since this leads to a combinatorial reduction. )

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: Suppose there is a triangle (i, k, j) with weight less than -Delta and let ell coloneqq S[i,j]. Then -Delta > A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] ge A[i,k] + B[k,j] + U[i,ell] + V[ell,j] - Delta/2 = A_ell[i,k] - B_ell[k,j] - Delta. So A_ell[i,k] < B_ell[k,j] and the triangle (i, k, j) will be detected in the dominance product. On the other hand, for any (i, k, j) with S[i,j] = ell and A_ell[i,k] < B_ell[k,j], we have 0 > A_ell[i,k] - B_ell[k,j] ge A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] and thus A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] < 0. Therefore, if the algorithm outputs (i, k, j), it must be negative

blocks.heading: Running Time.
blocks.text: There are 5r iterations. In each iteration we compute a single dominance product via a single invocation of the fast Integer APSP algorithm, in time tilde O(n^(3-epsilon)). The total running time hence becomes tilde O(r n^(3-epsilon)), as claimed. proof

blocks.heading: Doubling Reduction for Real APSP
blocks.text: In this section, we prove the edge weight reduction ( ), which allows us to transform any approximately low-rank matrix into an approximately uniform and low-doubling matrix with a potential-adjusting reduction. Except for the Delta -approximate part, the same chain of reductions was already carried out by Fischer [Fischer26] for the purpose of a universe reduction for APSP. Many intermediate steps are in turn based on a chain of reductions for APSP with a truly sublinear number of distinct edge weights per node [AbboudFJVX25]. We mostly have to follow the same reductions and proofs as in [Fischer26] in the approximate real setting. For our use cases, some steps can be slightly shortened or presented in a slightly less general way; whenever possible, we take the opportunity to do so. However, there are no big conceptual differences

blocks.heading: Low-Rank to Slice-Uniform
blocks.text: Let Delta in Realnneg and d in [n]. We call a matrix A in (Real cup bot )^(n times n) (d, Delta) -slice-uniform if the non- bot entries of either each row or each column in A have a Delta -cover of size at most d. An instance (A, B, C) is called (d, Delta) -slice-uniform if at least one of A, B, and C is (d, Delta) -slice-uniform

blocks.heading: Low-Rank to Slice-Uniform
blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Reduction from Approximately Low-Rank to Approximately Slice-Uniform Instances] For any t ge 1, there is a potential-adjusting reduction from a Real Exact Triangle Delta -approximate rank- r instance (A, B, C) to O(t^2 log r) (r, Delta) -slice-uniform instances. It runs in time tilde O ens*( n^3 (t) + n^2rt^2). end-of-lemma start-of-proof: Assume we are given a Delta -approximate rank- r decomposition (U, V, S) of the matrix C, otherwise simply rotate the instance. Furthermore, we may assume that for some R = O(log n), and for all ell in [r] and i in [n], we have |set(j in [n]: S[i,j] = ell)| le R cdot frac(n)(r), that is, each inner dimension of the rank decomposition is selected the same number of times per row up to factors of O(log n) (see [Lemmas 3.5 and 4.4, Fischer26] for the corresponding unchanged arguments of this assumption). Let T gets emptyset be the set of exceptional triples, and let I gets emptyset be the set of (r, Delta) -slice-uniform potential adjustments of (A, B, C). Consider the algorithm that enumerates ell gets 1, ldots, r. In iteration ell, we ensure that each Delta -approximate exact triangle (i, k, j) with S[i,j] = ell is either inserted into T or still present in an instance in I. start-of-enumerate:. (Heavy/Light Setup) Define matrices A_ell and B_ell of size n times n by A_ell[i,k] &coloneqq A[i,k] + U[i,ell], B_ell[k,j] &coloneqq -(B[k,j] + V[ell, j]). Note that this way for all pairs (i, j) with S[i,j] = ell, the condition A[i,k] + B[k,j] + C[i,j] = 0 pm Delta implies A_ell[i,k] = B_ell[k,j] pm 2Delta. For the remainder of this algorithm, we classify the non- bot entries of A_ell as either light or heavy. We call a non- bot entry (i, k) light if abs(set(i' in [n]: A_ell[i,k] = A_ell[i',k] pm 4Delta)) le frac(n)(rt) and heavy otherwise. Creating A_ell and B_ell and classifying entries as either heavy or light takes time tilde O(n^2r) across all r iterations.. (Light Edges) We enumerate all triples (i, k, j) with A_ell[i,k] = B_ell[k,j] pm 2Delta for which (i, k) is light as follows. Enumerate all pairs (k, j) in [n]^2. If there exists a light edge (i', k) with A_ell[i',k] = B_ell[k,j] pm 2Delta, enumerate all rows i with A_ell[i,k] = B_ell[k,j]pm 2Delta. There are at most n/(rt) such rows, since each satisfies A_ell[i,k] = A_ell[i',k]pm 4Delta and (i', k) is light. We insert each such triple into T. This step correctly deals with all Delta -approximate solutions involving light edges in time tilde O(n^3/t+n^2r) across all r iterations.. (Heavy Edges) We distinguish two cases depending on the number of heavy edges: start-of-enumerate:. (Few Heavy Edges) If there are at most n^2/t heavy edges, we can enumerate all relevant triples by brute force as follows. Enumerate all heavy pairs (i, k) in [n]^2, and enumerate all columns j in [n] with S[i,j] = ell. Each enumerated triple (i, k, j) that forms a Delta -approximate exact triangle is inserted into T. This clearly takes care of all heavy triples. By the initial regularity assumptions of the rank decomposition, for each i in [n], there are at most tilde O(n/r) columns j with S[i,j] = ell. Hence, the running time of this step is tilde O(n^2/t cdot n/r) and thus tilde O(n^3/t) across all iterations.. (Many Heavy Edges) The final case is that there are more than n^2 / t heavy pairs. Let A_H be the matrix A restricted to the heavy pairs (all other entries are set to bot ). We take care of the full instance (A_H, B, C) using potential-adjustments and afterwards globally remove all heavy entries from A. Construct matrices A' and C' by A'[i,k] &coloneqq A[i,k] + U[i,ell], &text(if (i, k) is heavy, ), &text(otherwise; ) C'[i,j] &coloneqq C[i,j] - U[i,ell]. By definition, (A', B, C') is a potential-adjusting restriction of (A, B, C) and retains all heavy exact triangle solutions. Furthermore, A' is (4rt, Delta) -slice-uniform. To see this, in each column greedily select the leftmost uncovered heavy value a and cover all heavy values in [a,a+8Delta] by four intervals of width 2Delta. The selected values are more than 8Delta apart, so their neighborhoods [a-4Delta,a+4Delta] are disjoint. Each neighborhood contains more than n/(rt) entries of A_ell, hence there are at most rt selections and at most 4rt cover intervals. Then, we trivially reduce (A', B, C') to 4t instances that are (r, Delta) -slice-uniform and insert these instances in I. This way we have dealt with all triangles (i, k, j) where (i, k) is heavy. Therefore, we can safely assign all heavy entries A[i,k] to bot for all future iterations. Regarding the running time, constructing the slice-uniform instances takes near-linear time in the output tilde O(n^2t) and adds O(t) instances to I. Since there are at least n^2/t heavy edges and we remove them globally after the iteration, we execute this step at most t times in total. Therefore, across all iterations, the running time of this step is bounded by tilde O(n^2t^2) and I le 4t^2. end-of-enumerate end-of-enumerate The correctness and running time of the reduction are already analyzed per step. In total, the running time is bounded by tilde O(n^3/t + n^2rt^2), as claimed. With the initial regularity assumption, the number of created instances is bounded by O(t^2 log r). end-of-proof

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: For property (i), consider any sum z in P_(2s)^(pm Delta)(X, Y). There are at least 2s pairs (x, y) in X times Y with x + y = z pm Delta. By Chernoff's bound, we have sampled at least 1. 5R such pairs in S with high probability. Let a and b be the smallest and largest sampled sums in [z-Delta,z+Delta]. Both b-Delta and a+Delta belong to Q, and their width- 2Delta intervals contain all these sampled sums, so both enter P. Since zin[b-Delta,a+Delta] and this interval has length at most 2Delta, at least one of these centers is within Delta of z. A union bound over at most |X||Y| possible sums z proves property (i). Similarly, consider any z in X + Y + -Delta, 0, Delta for which there are at most s choices of (x, y) in Xtimes Y with x + y = z pm Delta. Chernoff's bound again shows that there will be at most 1. 1R such pairs sampled in S with high probability. Therefore, conditioned on this event, z itself is not in P. Since Psubseteq Qsubseteq X + Y + -Delta, 0, Delta, a union bound over this fixed set of at most 3|X||Y| possible centers proves property (ii)

blocks.text: start-of-lemma: [Popular Sum Decomposition] Let Delta in Realnneg, let X_1, dots, X_n, Y_1, dots, Y_n subseteq Real be Omega(Delta) -spaced sets of size at most d, and let p geq 1. Then there exist an integer m=O(p^2) and partitions X_i &= X_i^* sqcup bigsqcup_(g=1)^(m) X_(i, g), Y_j &= Y_j^* sqcup bigsqcup_(h=1)^(m) Y_(j, h) satisfying the following two properties: start-of-enumerate: [label=( )]. There are sets S_g subseteq Real of size |S_g| leq d and shifts s_(i, g) in Real such that S_g + s_(i, g) is a Delta -cover for X_(i, g) (for all i in [n], g in [m] ), and there are sets T_h subseteq Real of size |T_h| leq d and shifts t_(j, h) in Real such that T_h + t_(j, h) is a Delta -cover for Y_(j, h) (for all j in [n], h in [m] ).. abs(set((i, j) in [n]^2: P^(pmDelta)_(2d / p)(X_i^*, Y_j) neq emptyset)) leq n^2 / p, and abs(set((i, j) in [n]^2: P^(pmDelta)_(2d / p)(X_i, Y_j^*) neq emptyset)) leq n^2 / p. end-of-enumerate Moreover, there is an algorithm that, given the sets X_i, Y_j, computes the partitions along with the sets S_g, T_h and the shifts s_(i, g), t_(j, h) in randomized time tilde O(n^2dp^3). end-of-lemma proof We show how to construct the partitions of the sets X_i and the S_g and s_(i, g); the other part is symmetric. Fix a constant c_0ge1 such that all X_i and Y_j are Delta/c_0 -spaced. Every interval of width 2Delta then contains at most 2c_0+1 elements of any one of these sets. Consider the algorithm that runs the following steps for g = 1, 2, dots: start-of-enumerate:. Apply with parameter d/p. For each (i, j) in [n]^2, it computes a set P_(i, j) subseteq Real that is a Delta -cover of P_(2d/p)^(pm Delta)(X_i, Y_j) and each p in P_(i, j) covers sums from at least d/p pairs in X_itimes Y_j.. If abs(set((i, j) in [n]^2: P_(i, j) ne emptyset)) le n^2/p, pick X_i^* coloneqq X_i for all i in [n] and stop the algorithm.. Otherwise, pick some j in [n] for which there are at least n/p many i in [n] such that P_(i, j) ne emptyset. Choose S_g coloneqq -Y_j. We call an index i good if P_(i, j) ne emptyset and bad otherwise. For each bad i, choose X_(i, g) coloneqq emptyset and s_(i, g) arbitrarily. For each good i, instead pick an arbitrary cover center s_(i, g) in P_(i, j). Then, pick X_(i, g) coloneqq X_i cap bigcup_(s in S_g) [s + s_(i,g) - Delta, s+s_(i,g) + Delta], that is, as the set of elements in X_i that are covered by a number in S_g + s_(i, g). Afterwards, remove X_(i, g) from X_i and continue with the next iteration. end-of-enumerate

blocks.heading: Correctness.
blocks.text: All properties are trivially satisfied after the algorithm terminates except for g=O(c_0p^2)=O(p^2), which we show in the following. Consider iteration g and suppose we chose index j. Let i be a good index. We claim that X_(i, g) has size at least d/((2c_0+1)p). For each fixed xin X_i, the spacing of Y_j allows at most 2c_0+1 elements yin Y_j with x+y=s_(i, g)pmDelta. Thus each covered element of X_i accounts for at most 2c_0+1 of the representing pairs. Indeed by the choice of s_(i, g) in P_(i, j), we have that abs(X_(i, g)) = big| X_i cap bigcup_(s in S_g) [s + s_(i,g) - Delta, s+s_(i,g) + Delta]big| ge frac(abs(set((x, y)in X_itimes Y_j: x+y=s_(i, g)pmDelta)))(2c_0+1) ge frac(d)((2c_0+1)p)

blocks.heading: Outer Regularization
blocks.text: We start with a preprocessing step that allows us to assume afterwards that each element in the Delta -cover covers roughly the same number of elements in each row of A and column of B. To this end, we partition A into L = lceil log n rceil matrices A_0, ldots, A_L where we include in the matrix A_ell all entries A[i,k] for which there are between 2^ell and 2^(ell + 1) entries A[i,k'] in its row with A[i,k'] = A[i,k] pm Delta. Similarly, we partition B into B_0, ldots, B_L according to the number of approximately equal column entries. We are left with (L+1)^2 instances (A_ell, B_(ell'), C) for 0 le ell, ell' le L. For the remainder of the proof, fix one such instance and write A = A_ell and B = B_(ell') for simplicity of notation. For each i in [n], compute the greedy minimum Delta -cover X_i for the i -th row of A and also compute the greedy minimum Delta -cover Y_j for the entries of the j -th column of B for each j in [n]. Let d_A coloneqq min d, n/2^ell and d_B coloneqq n/2^(ell') and note that for each row i of A, we have that |X_i| le d_A. The same claim holds for columns of B with |Y_j| le d_B. We finally argue that we may also assume that d_B le d_Acdot t in the following. Indeed, if d_B > d_A cdot t, we can enumerate all solutions in the instance efficiently as follows. Enumerate all pairs (i, j) in [n]^2, enumerate all of the at most d_A elements x in X_i, and enumerate all k in [n] with B[k,j] = - C[i,j] - x pm 2Delta. Insert all enumerated triangles (i, k, j) into T

blocks.heading: Outer Regularization
blocks.text: We take care of all Delta -approximate exact triangles in this step if the assumptions are not met. Indeed, if (i, k, j) is a Delta -approximate exact triangle, then B[k,j] = -C[i,j] - A[i,k] pm Delta, and because A[i,k] = x pm Delta, we have also B[k,j] = -C[i,j] - x pm 2Delta. Therefore, this step is correct. For the running time, notice that there are only |X_i| le d_A many elements x per row to enumerate. For each cover element, there are only constantly many elements y in Y_j to enumerate that would complete a Delta -approximate exact triangle. Each such y covers at most O(n/d_B) values B[k,j].
